analysis.one_liner: Makes the low capital gains and dividend tax rates permanent and cuts the estate tax for large estates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced in May 2008 with no cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lock in, permanently, the low 15% tax rates on capital gains and dividends that were set to rise after 2010. It would also spare estates up to $3.5 million from the estate tax and tax everything above that at a flat 15%, instead of the higher estate tax rates then scheduled to return. Both changes reduce taxes mainly owed by households with large investments or large estates.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who hold stocks paying dividends, and heirs of large estates. The 15% capital gains and dividends rates flow mostly to households in the top income brackets, since that is where most investment income sits. The estate tax change exempts estates under $3.5 million entirely and taxes amounts above it at 15% rather than the 45% rate scheduled for 2010, so the savings grow with the size of the estate.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the reduced tax rates on capital gains and dividends enacted in 2003, which otherwise were scheduled to expire after 2010 [S2][S3].
Restores and sets the estate and gift tax exclusion at $3.5 million per person, shielding estates up to that size from any estate tax after 2009, with the threshold adjusted for inflation [S2][S3].
Sets a single flat 15% rate on taxable estates and gifts, replacing the top rate of 45% scheduled to return in 2010, so the largest estates pay far less than under current law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and with it the general body of taxpayers, since the revenue from capital gains, dividends, and large estates would be permanently reduced. Under the tax law then in effect, rates were set to revert to higher levels; this bill cancels that reversion [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: General federal taxpayers through lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The savings concentrate at the top: most capital gains, dividends, and taxable estates belong to high-income households, so cutting those taxes shifts the tax burden toward wages and smaller estates [S2][S3].

Making the 2003 rates permanent removes the sunset that Congress built into the 2001 and 2003 tax laws precisely to cap their long-run cost, turning temporary reductions into a permanent loss of federal revenue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real, permanent tax cut, but nearly all of it goes to households with large investment portfolios and large estates. The cost is permanent federal revenue that would otherwise have returned in 2011, borne by taxpayers broadly. For someone whose income comes from a paycheck and whose estate is far below $3.5 million, the bill offers little benefit and its fiscal cost is real.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Lamar Alexander introduced the bill in the Senate on May 22, 2008 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was its last official action [S5].
The Finance Committee never considered it, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax and the scheduled rise in capital gains and dividends rates stayed on the books, preserving federal revenue that would otherwise have been permanently cut for the largest estates and investment portfolios.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; large-estate investors gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee; the bill's only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation (chaired by Sen. Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill after referring it in May 2008; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its only sponsor was a Republican and no senator of either party cosponsored it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would permanently lock in the 15% rates on capital gains and dividends and cut the estate tax to 15% above a $3.5 million exemption, changes whose benefits scale with the size of a portfolio or estate. The cost — permanent federal revenue loss — falls on the general tax base.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: A larger exemption and a flat 15% rate would simplify estate planning and reduce tax bills for wealthy clients, but a less punitive estate tax also shrinks the demand for elaborate tax-avoidance structures that the estate tax currently drives.
